summary: The bill creates a new reinsurance program funded at up to $6 billion per year through 2030 to reimburse high-cost claims in off-Exchange individual health plans that opt out of the ACA single risk pool, allows those plans to set age-based premiums without the usual 3:1 limit, and requires out-of-network costs to count toward deductibles plus price disclosure to patients.

scores.thoughts: This bill primarily focuses on modifying the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act to establish a reinsurance program for certain off-Exchange plans, allow issuers to opt out of the single risk pool for these plans, and remove age premium variation limitations for them. It also includes provisions for applying out-of-network costs to deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums and requiring disclosure of lower prices by healthcare providers. These changes aim to alter the structure and regulation of private health insurance markets, moving towards more private sector flexibility and potentially less government oversight in certain areas, while also introducing some consumer protections related to cost transparency.

The bill explicitly states that no funds from the reinsurance program may be used for services described in section 1303(b)(1)(B)(i) of the ACA, which refers to abortion services. This provision directly restricts federal funding from being used for abortion, aligning with a pro-life stance.

The bill creates a new federal reinsurance program funded by direct Treasury appropriations of up to $6 billion annually from 2026-2030 with no offsets, increasing federal spending and the deficit. This spending provision is a notable but secondary element within a broader health-insurance reform bill.

The core of the bill establishes a reinsurance program for off-exchange plans, permits issuers to opt out of single-risk-pool and age-rating rules, and adds price-disclosure and out-of-network cost protections—all designed to foster market competition and lower premiums outside the ACA framework.
